content.text: predict_proba

returns scores between 0 and 1 that sum to one, not a guarantee of probabilities. A 0.8 means 80% only if the model is calibrated: among all the cases it scores near 0.8, about 80% are positive. Here, reports a naive Bayes model scored under 5% were 13.7% violations. Check scores with a calibration curve, fix them with
CalibratedClassifierCV
, and the ranking stays the same.

A trust and safety team uses a classifier on its queue of reported posts. To save reviewer time, it auto-dismisses any report the model scores under 5%, an error rate everyone agreed to. The model's ROC AUC is a solid 0.934. Three months later an audit samples the dismissed reports: 13.7% of them broke the rules. The model said those reports had a 0.2% chance on average. Nobody had checked whether its numbers meant what they said.
The common misconception
Many developers read
predict_proba
as the chance a prediction is right: a 0.8 means an 80% chance. It's an easy belief to hold:

items.text: The method is literally called
predict_proba
, and its output behaves like probabilities: between 0 and 1, summing to 1 across classes.
Logistic regression, the first classifier most people learn, often does give well-calibrated probabilities, so the habit forms early.
Good accuracy and ROC AUC feel like they certify everything the model outputs.

content.text: The half-truth: for some models, under some conditions, the outputs are good probabilities. But nothing in the API promises it. Whether a 0.8 means 80% is an empirical property of a model on a data distribution, and you have to measure it.
What actually happens

A classifier is trained to separate classes, and its scores only have to put the cases in the right order for that. Turning those scores into honest frequencies is a separate property with its own name.
Calibration is a statement about groups
scikit-learn's calibration guide defines it: a well-calibrated binary classifier is one where, among the samples it gives a
predict_proba

close to 0.8, about 80% actually belong to the positive class. That's a claim about a group of cases checked against outcomes, never about a single case. A calibrated 0.8 means "8 in 10 cases like this one". It also says nothing about how useful the model is: one that gave every case the base rate would be perfectly
calibrated
and useless. Ranking and calibration are two separate qualities, and a model can have either without the other.
Why scores drift from frequencies
Each model family distorts in its own way:

items.text: Naive Bayes
assumes features are independent given the class. When several features carry the same evidence, it counts that evidence several times and pushes scores toward 0 and 1.
Max-margin methods
such as SVMs and boosted trees push scores away from 0 and 1, a sigmoid-shaped distortion described by Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana; scikit-learn's guide shows random forests rarely reaching 0 or 1.
Modern neural networks
are often poorly calibrated, Guo and colleagues found, and they link it to depth, width, weight decay and batch normalization.
Class weights and resampling
change the class balance the model learns from, so its scores describe that rebalanced world, not yours.

content.text: Logistic regression is the friendly exception: the guide credits its log loss and logit link, provided the model fits the data well. In the example below, 10 of the 20 features are mixes of the 2 informative ones, the textbook trap for naive Bayes.

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB

# 2 informative features plus 10 redundant mixes of them
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, n_features=20, n_informative=2,
                           n_redundant=10, random_state=11)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=0)
proba = GaussianNB().fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
low = proba < 0.05  # auto-dismissed as "under 5% likely"
print(f"under 5%: {low.sum()} reports, {y_te[low].mean():.1%} violating")
share, score = calibration_curve(y_te, proba, n_bins=5)
print("mean score    ", score.round(2))
print("share positive", share.round(2))
auc, brier = roc_auc_score(y_te, proba), brier_score_loss(y_te, proba)
print(f"ROC AUC {auc:.3f}, Brier {brier:.3f}")
# under 5%: 5078 reports, 13.7% violating
# mean score     [0.01 0.3  0.5  0.71 0.99]
# share positive [0.16 0.55 0.57 0.7  0.93]
# ROC AUC 0.934, Brier 0.121

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV, calibration_curve
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20_000, n_features=20, n_informative=2,
                           n_redundant=10, random_state=11)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=0)
model = CalibratedClassifierCV(GaussianNB(), method="isotonic", cv=5)
proba = model.fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
low = proba < 0.05
print(f"under 5%: {low.sum()} reports, {y_te[low].mean():.1%} violating")
share, score = calibration_curve(y_te, proba, n_bins=5)
print("mean score    ", score.round(2))
print("share positive", share.round(2))
auc, brier = roc_auc_score(y_te, proba), brier_score_loss(y_te, proba)
print(f"ROC AUC {auc:.3f}, Brier {brier:.3f}")
# under 5%: 1839 reports, 4.7% violating
# mean score     [0.08 0.3  0.52 0.75 0.95]
# share positive [0.08 0.31 0.52 0.75 0.95]
# ROC AUC 0.934, Brier 0.098

content.text: The
calibration curve

tells the story. The raw model's lowest bin averages a score of 0.01, yet 16% of those cases are positive; its top bin averages 0.99 and is 93% positive. That's the overconfident shape naive Bayes is known for. After isotonic calibration, each bin's mean score matches its share of positives within a point. The 5% rule now dismisses 1,839 reports instead of 5,078, and 4.7% of them violate, the error rate the team signed up for. It automates less, but its number finally means what it says.
ROC AUC is 0.934 both times. The calibration example in scikit-learn explains why: calibration is a monotonic transformation, so rank metrics aren't affected. The
Brier score
drops from 0.121 to 0.098. The guide adds a caution: Brier score and log loss mix calibration with discrimination, so a lower value doesn't prove better calibration on its own. Look at the curve.
How CalibratedClassifierCV fits
With
cv=5

, it fits a copy of the classifier on four fifths of the training data and fits the calibrator on the remaining fifth, five times, then averages the five calibrated models' probabilities. The calibrator never sees scores from rows the classifier trained on. Pick the method by your data:

items.text: "sigmoid"
is Platt's method: a logistic regression on the scores, with few parameters, good for small data and sigmoid-shaped distortions.
"isotonic"
fits any monotonic distortion, but the API reference warns it tends to overfit with well under 1,000 calibration samples.
"temperature"
, added in scikit-learn 1.8, divides the logits by one fitted value, and handles multiclass natively.

rows.text: It returns scores; they're probabilities only if calibrated, which you measure
A 0.8 means this case is 80% likely
A calibrated 0.8 means about 8 in 10 cases scored like it are positive
High ROC AUC means trustworthy scores
ROC AUC stayed 0.934; calibration is monotonic
Calibration holds for the data it was fit on; recheck when the base rate shifts

blocks.title: Check the curve before you trust a number

content.text: Run
calibration_curve
, or
CalibrationDisplay.from_estimator
, on held-out data before any rule or report uses a score as a probability. Look at the counts per bin too: a bin with 30 cases can wander far from the diagonal by chance.

blocks.title: Never fit the calibrator on the training rows

content.text: A model looks surer than it should on rows it trained on, so a calibrator fit there learns the wrong correction. The guide says the calibrator should ideally be fit on data independent of the classifier's training data: use
cv
, or wrap an already trained model in
FrozenEstimator
and calibrate it on a held-out set.
How to apply it in your project
Ranking, or a cut-off tuned on validation data, works with any scores. Expected values, displayed confidence and fixed probability rules need calibration.

items.title: Plot the curve on held-out data

content.text: Use
calibration_curve
with the counts per bin, for the model exactly as it's deployed.
Use sigmoid for small calibration sets, isotonic with more than about 1,000 samples, temperature for multiclass.

items.title: Evaluate on data the calibrator never saw

content.text: Report the curve with log loss or Brier score from a separate test split.
A new base rate, a new market or retraining with class weights can break calibration silently. Plot the curve on recent data.
Key takeaways

items.text: predict_proba
gives scores; a 0.8 means 80% only if the model is calibrated, and that's something you measure.
Calibration is about groups: of all cases scored 0.8, about 80% should be positive.
Naive Bayes, max-margin models, deep networks and class weights all distort scores; here "under 5%" meant 13.7%.
CalibratedClassifierCV
fixed it without changing the ranking: ROC AUC stayed 0.934.
